questions.q: What problem does state locking solve that remote state alone does not?
options: It makes terraform apply run faster
It prevents two apply runs from touching the same state file at the same time
It encrypts the state file
It automatically fixes drift
questions.explain: Remote state gives a team one shared file, but by itself does nothing to stop two people writing to it simultaneously. Locking is what prevents that collision.

questions.q: In the s3 backend, what is the dynamodb_table setting used for?
options: Storing the actual infrastructure resources being provisioned
Holding lock records so a second apply can detect that one is already running
Caching the Terraform provider plugins
Billing and cost tracking
questions.explain: The DynamoDB table referenced by dynamodb_table exists purely to hold lock records, letting Terraform detect that an apply is already in progress.

questions.q: How does the azurerm backend implement state locking?
options: It requires a separate DynamoDB-equivalent resource to be created manually
It locks natively using a lease placed directly on the state blob -- no extra resource needed
It does not support locking at all
It locks by deleting the state file during an apply
questions.explain: Unlike the s3 backend, the azurerm backend locks natively via a lease on the state blob itself, with no separate lock resource required.

questions.q: What does the 'Error acquiring the state lock' message tell the engineer who sees it?
options: That the state file has been permanently corrupted
Who currently holds the lock, which operation they're running, and when it started
That their internet connection failed
That the resource they're trying to create already exists in Azure
questions.explain: The Lock Info output names the holder, the operation (such as apply), and the timestamp, so the blocked engineer knows exactly who to check in with.

questions.q: Without state locking, what is the realistic risk of two engineers running terraform apply at the same moment?
options: Nothing -- Terraform always serializes applies automatically regardless of locking
Both applies read the same starting state, make conflicting changes, and the second write can silently overwrite the first, corrupting state
The second apply crashes the Terraform CLI permanently
Azure and AWS billing doubles
questions.explain: Without a lock, two simultaneous applies have no way to coordinate -- the second write can overwrite the first, leaving state that no longer reflects reality.
